messages.content: What is feature engineering and why does it matter?

Feature engineering: transforming raw data into representations that make it easier for models to learn patterns. Often more impactful than model selection. Techniques: encoding categorical variables (one-hot, target encoding), creating interaction features (feature A × feature B), polynomial features (A²), date/time decomposition (day of week, hour, seasonality flags), domain-specific transformations (log-transform skewed distributions, normalise), binning continuous variables, aggregating from child to parent entities. A simple model on well-engineered features often outperforms a complex model on raw features. Data quality and representation beat model sophistication.
What is A/B testing and how do you design one correctly?

A/B testing randomly assigns users to control (A) vs treatment (B) group and measures the effect of a change on a metric. Design correctly: define hypothesis and metric before starting (pre-registration prevents p-hacking), calculate required sample size for desired statistical power (typically 80%) at expected effect size, ensure random assignment is truly random, run for sufficient time to capture weekly cycles, check for novelty effects. Common mistakes: stopping early when you see a significant result (false positive inflation), running multiple variations without correcting for multiple comparisons, testing on non-representative traffic.
What is the bias-variance tradeoff in machine learning?

A model's total error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias: systematic error from incorrect assumptions in the model — high bias = underfitting (model too simple, misses patterns). Variance: sensitivity to small fluctuations in training data — high variance = overfitting (model memorises training data, fails to generalise). Tradeoff: as model complexity increases, bias decreases (fits training data better) but variance increases (overfit to training noise). Optimal: find the complexity level that minimises total test error. Regularisation, cross-validation, and more training data help manage this tradeoff.
How do you handle missing data in a dataset?

Options: Complete case analysis (drop rows with missing values) — only appropriate if missing completely at random and proportion is small (<5%). Single imputation (replace with mean/median/mode) — creates false certainty, underestimates variance. Multiple imputation — generate several imputed datasets, analyse each, pool results — gold standard for random missing data. Model-based imputation (predict missing value from other features). For ML: some algorithms (XGBoost) handle missing values natively. Key question first: is data missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random (MAR), or missing not at random (MNAR)? The mechanism determines the appropriate method.
